topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: New York's Property Condition Disclosure Act (PCDA), codified at RPL Article 14, Sections 460-467, has required sellers of what type of property to complete a Property Condition Disclosure Statement (PCDS) since 2002?
explanation: Since 2002, the PCDA has required sellers of one-to-four family residential dwellings to deliver a completed Property Condition Disclosure Statement to the buyer, disclosing known property conditions.
source_note: RPL Article 14, Sections 460-467 (Property Condition Disclosure Act)

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Effective March 20, 2024, a significant amendment to the Property Condition Disclosure Act eliminated what previously available option for sellers who did not want to complete the PCDS?
choice_a: The option to sell the property without a real estate broker
choice_b: The option to use a licensed attorney instead of a broker
choice_c: The option to instead provide the buyer a $500 credit at closing in lieu of completing the disclosure statement
choice_d: The option to close the transaction remotely
explanation: Effective March 20, 2024, an amendment signed by Governor Hochul in September 2023 eliminated the prior Section 465(1) option letting a seller provide a $500 credit at closing instead of completing the PCDS -- effectively making the disclosure statement itself mandatory in nearly all covered transactions.
source_note: RPL Section 465(1), as amended effective March 20, 2024 (elimination of $500 credit option)

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: The same 2024 PCDA amendment added new required disclosure questions covering what subject area, in response to increased attention to climate-related risk?
choice_d: Flood hazard areas, federal flood insurance requirements, FEMA assistance history, and flood insurance claims
explanation: The 2024 amendment added seven new PCDS questions addressing flood-related risk -- including whether the property sits within a FEMA 100-year or 500-year floodplain, federal flood insurance requirements, prior FEMA disaster assistance, current flood insurance coverage, FEMA elevation certificates, and any flood-related insurance claims.
source_note: RPL Article 14, as amended effective March 20, 2024 (flood-related disclosure questions)

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Approximately how many total questions does the amended PCDS form contain, up from 49 questions on the prior version?
explanation: The 2024 amendment expanded the PCDS from 49 questions to 56 questions, primarily by adding the new flood-related disclosure items.
source_note: RPL Article 14, as amended effective March 20, 2024 (56-question PCDS)

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Which of the following environmental conditions is specifically addressed on New York's Property Condition Disclosure Statement?
choice_a: The property's current market value as determined by a licensed appraiser
choice_b: Whether a radon test has been performed on the property, and if so, whether a copy of the report is attached
choice_d: The broker's commission rate on the transaction
explanation: The PCDS specifically asks whether a radon test has been performed and requires attaching the report if one exists, alongside other environmental items such as asbestos, lead pipes, underground fuel storage tanks, wetlands/flood plain/agricultural district location, and known hazardous substance spills or releases.
source_note: DOS Form 1614-f (Property Condition Disclosure Statement) -- environmental hazard questions

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Is the completed PCDS a warranty by the seller that the disclosed conditions are the only conditions affecting the property?
choice_a: Yes -- once signed, the PCDS legally warrants the property is free of any undisclosed defect
choice_b: Yes, but only for defects costing more than $10,000 to repair
choice_c: No -- the disclosure statement reflects conditions known to the seller and is explicitly not a warranty, and is not a substitute for the buyer's own inspections
choice_d: The PCDS replaces the need for a home inspection entirely
explanation: The PCDS form itself explicitly states that it reflects conditions known to the seller, is not a warranty of any kind by the seller or the seller's agent, and is not a substitute for a buyer's own home, pest, radon, or other inspections -- buyers should still conduct independent due diligence.
source_note: DOS Form 1614-f (Property Condition Disclosure Statement) -- express non-warranty language

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Federal law requires disclosure of lead-based paint hazards for residential properties built before what year?
explanation: Federal law (implementing the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act) requires sellers and landlords of housing built before 1978 to disclose known lead-based paint hazards and provide an EPA-approved pamphlet to buyers/tenants -- a separate requirement layered on top of New York's own PCDS.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement (applies alongside PCDA in New York)

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Which of the following does the PCDS ask a seller to disclose regarding the property's location relative to environmentally sensitive or hazard-prone areas?
choice_a: Whether the property is within a flood plain, wetlands, or an agricultural district, or near a landfill
choice_b: Whether the seller has ever attended a local zoning board meeting
choice_c: Whether the seller's mortgage lender is headquartered in New York
choice_d: Whether the seller has ever hired a real estate photographer
explanation: The PCDS specifically asks the seller to disclose whether the property is located within a flood plain, wetlands, or agricultural district, or is near a landfill -- items with meaningful implications for development restrictions, insurance costs, and future use.
source_note: DOS Form 1614-f (Property Condition Disclosure Statement) -- location-based environmental disclosures

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Does an underground storage tank on the property need to be disclosed on the PCDS?
choice_a: No -- underground storage tanks are outside the scope of the PCDS entirely
choice_b: Yes -- underground storage tanks (such as old fuel oil tanks) are specifically among the environmental items the PCDS requires the seller to disclose
choice_c: Only if the tank has been removed within the last 30 days
choice_d: Only if the buyer specifically asks about it in writing before contract
explanation: Underground storage tanks (a common issue with older heating-oil systems) are specifically among the environmental hazard categories the PCDS asks a seller to disclose, alongside asbestos, lead pipes, and known contamination.
source_note: DOS Form 1614-f (Property Condition Disclosure Statement) -- underground storage tank disclosure

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Now that the $500 credit alternative has been eliminated, what is the practical significance for a broker representing a seller who is reluctant to complete the PCDS?
choice_a: Nothing has changed -- the $500 credit alternative is still fully available under current law
choice_b: The broker may simply complete the PCDS on the seller's behalf without the seller's knowledge or review
choice_c: The broker should advise the seller (in coordination with the seller's attorney) that completing the PCDS is now effectively required, since the prior 'opt-out' credit alternative no longer exists under the amended law
choice_d: The broker should advise the seller that no disclosure is required for any transaction after March 2024
explanation: Because the March 2024 amendment eliminated the $500 credit alternative, a broker's supervisory and advisory role now includes making clear to a reluctant seller (working with the seller's own attorney) that PCDS completion is effectively mandatory going forward, a materially different landscape than before the amendment.
source_note: RPL Section 465(1), as amended effective March 20, 2024 (broker advisory implications)

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Which agency's document (form DOS-1614-f) is the official New York Property Condition Disclosure Statement?
choice_b: The New York State Department of Financial Services
choice_c: The New York State Division of Human Rights
choice_d: The New York Department of State
explanation: The official Property Condition Disclosure Statement is published by the New York Department of State as form DOS-1614-f, distinct from federal disclosure forms (like the EPA lead-based paint pamphlet) that also apply to New York transactions.

topic: Property Condition Disclosure Act & Environmental Issues
question: Why did the 2023-2024 PCDA amendment specifically add flood-related disclosure questions, given New York's broader regulatory trends?
choice_a: To improve buyer awareness of flood risk and insurance obligations in light of increasing climate-related flood exposure and FEMA floodplain mapping relevance to property transactions
choice_b: Because flood risk had never previously been a concern anywhere in New York State
choice_c: To replace the need for any separate flood insurance policy
choice_d: Because federal law required New York to remove all environmental disclosure questions
explanation: The added flood-related questions reflect a broader legislative trend toward improving buyer awareness of climate-related risk -- helping buyers understand FEMA floodplain status, flood insurance obligations, and a property's flood claim history before committing to a purchase.
source_note: RPL Article 14, as amended effective March 20, 2024 (policy rationale for flood-disclosure additions)
